Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

say verb

also tell, tell me, they say, say no, give a negative answer, answer no, so they say, I have to say, this is what I have to say, I have nothing to say, I have nothing to write

classical

Ter. And. 762: Tibi ego dīcō, annōn?
Plaut. Men. 696: heus tū, tibi dīcō

dīcō, dīcere, dīxī, dictum

verb, third conjugation

say, tell

With an accusative and infinitive for what is said (dīcit sē ventūrum esse) and a dative of the person told: Dīc mihi, “tell me”; Tibi dīcō!, “I’m talking to you!” The imperative is dīc.

Other words

  • inquam, inquis, inquit — say, with the speaker’s own words

    verb, defective · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 5.1.3: ēn, inquit, mihi haec ego patior cotīdiē; Ter. Hec. 495–496: manē, inquam

    Only with direct speech, and never before it: it follows the first word or words, «Venī,» inquit, «mēcum.», or the first sentence, «Venī,» inquit. «Cēna parāta est.» After a repeated word it insists: manē, inquam, “wait, I said”.

  • ajō, ais, ait — say, say yes; ajunt, they say

    verb, defective · also used · classical · Ter. Eun. 252: Negat quis? negō: ait? ajō.; Ter. Ph. 419: Āctum, ajunt, nē agās.; Ter. And. 1.2.21: ita ajunt, so they say (Lewis & Short s.v. ita); Traupman 107: so they say, ita ajunt

    The opposite of negō. Ajunt, “they say”, brings in a saying; Quid ais? is “What do you say?” or “What’s that?”. For Ain' vērō? see really.

  • negō, negāre, negāvī, negātum — say no; say that … not

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 2.8.1: quaerō ecquid litterārum. negant.

    Latin for “say that … not”: negat sē ventūrum esse, he says he won’t come.

  • habeō (+ infinitive) — I have (something) to say, I can say

    also used · classical · Cic. Att. 2.22.6: dē rē pūblicā nihil habeō ad tē scrībere (Lewis & Short s.v. habeō); Cic. Rosc. Am. 100: habeō etiam dīcere (Lewis & Short); Traupman 100: this I have to say, haec habeō dīcere

    Like Greek ἔχω with the infinitive: to have something to do, to be able to. Not “I must”, which is the sense of later Latin (see must).

Examples

  • ecce tibi nūntius puerōs vēnisse Rōmā! vocō, quaerō ecquid litterārum. negant. quid ais? inquam, nihilne ā Pompōniō?

    And look: news that the couriers have come from Rome! I call them and ask if there’s a letter. They say no. “What?” I say, “nothing from Pomponius?”Cic. Att. 2.8.1

  • dabis poenās, nōn dīcō quās

    You’ll pay for it — I won’t say how.Plin. Ep. 1.15.3

  • Tibi ego dīcō, annōn? … Mitte id quod sciō: dīc quod rogō.

    I’m talking to you, aren’t I? … Never mind what I know: tell me what I’m asking.Ter. And. 762–764

  • Ita ajunt.

    So they say.Ter. And. 1.2.21 (Lewis & Short s.v. ita)

  • Haec habeō dīcere.

    This is what I have to say.Traupman 100

See also tell a story, say hello to … for me, give thanks, really?, talk, answer, negative, must.
